meta.title: Who really said "Happiness depends upon ourselves"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Aristotle never wrote it. The phrase is a connective clause added by translator J. A. K. Thomson in his 1955 Penguin Ethics — the Greek sentence it renders contains no word for 'happiness' and no word for 'ourselves'.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Happiness depends upon ourselves'?
meta.ogDescription: A translator's gloss, not Aristotle. The Greek at Nicomachean Ethics I.9 says only 'these things would agree with what was said at the beginning' — no happiness, no ourselves.

answer.label: Not Aristotle — a 1955 translator's gloss
answer.sourceLine: The words are J. A. K. Thomson’s, from his 1955 Penguin translation of the Nicomachean Ethics. Rendering a connective sentence at I.9, he wrote “The conclusion that happiness depends upon ourselves is in harmony with what I said in the first of these lectures” — supplying the italicised clause to tell the reader what ‘the conclusion’ was. The Greek sentence it translates contains no word for happiness and no word for ourselves.

source.heading: What Aristotle actually wrote

docMeta.dd: J. A. K. Thomson, The Ethics of Aristotle (Penguin, 1955)

source.excerpt: and this will be found to agree with what we said at the outset.
trail: The Greek at Nicomachean Ethics I.9 is a short connective sentence: ‘and these things would be in agreement with what was said at the beginning.’ W. D. Ross’s public-domain English renders it ‘and this will be found to agree with what we said at the outset’ — no happiness, no ourselves Ross translation ↗.

Thomson’s 1955 Penguin version expands it for clarity: ‘The conclusion that happiness depends upon ourselves is in harmony with what I said in the first of these lectures.’ The famous four words are the clause he added to identify the antecedent — a translator’s service to the reader, not a sentence of Aristotle’s Wikiquote, disputed ↗.

Stripped of Thomson’s surrounding sentence and printed as a standalone aphorism ‘— Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics,’ it acquires a citation it cannot support: there is no Greek line to point to Greek text, 1099b ↗.
source.excerptNote: Ross’s public-domain rendering of the sentence in question. Compare it with the famous four words — they are not a translation of it, they are an explanation inserted alongside it.
source.rightsNote: Split, and the split runs the wrong way for most people’s assumptions. Aristotle’s Greek is public domain — quote or translate it freely. But the four English words in circulation are Thomson’s 1955 translation, still in copyright (he died in 1959, so UK/EU protection runs to the end of 2029, and the US term for a 1955 publication runs considerably longer). Quote them as the object of analysis rather than as decoration. For free English on this passage use W. D. Ross’s Oxford translation, which is public domain in the United States — noting that Ross died in 1971, so life-plus-70 territories should check locally. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Aristotle
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Aristotle
author.bio: Aristotle did argue, at length, that eudaimonia is achieved through virtuous activity rather than luck or external goods — so ‘happiness depends upon ourselves’ is a fair four-word summary of a real position. That is exactly what makes it dangerous: it is not a distortion of his philosophy, it is a distillation of it, which is why nobody thinks to ask whether he ever wrote the sentence. He did not. His translator did.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is the purest example on the site of a category worth naming: a quotation that exists only in translation. The idea is genuinely Aristotle’s; the sentence was written in English in 1955.

items.why: Thomson added the clause to specify what ‘the conclusion’ referred to. It is an editorial kindness to the reader, not a rendering of any Greek phrase Wikiquote ↗.

The line at I.9 contains no word for happiness (eudaimonia) and none for ourselves. Ross’s translation of the same sentence reads simply ‘and this will be found to agree with what we said at the outset’ Ross ↗.

Quote sites append the work title, implying a locatable passage. There is none. Sources also disagree on the exact Bekker line for the sentence Thomson was translating, which is a further sign nobody quoting it has looked.

misattribution.truthLine: Not Aristotle’s words. The phrase is a clause J. A. K. Thomson supplied in his 1955 Penguin translation of Nicomachean Ethics I.9 — and it remains in copyright the finding ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It states the most attractive claim in ancient ethics in four words: that a good life is something you make rather than something you are given. Aristotle does argue close to this — happiness as activity of the soul in accordance with virtue, not a gift of fortune.

But he is also careful in ways the aphorism is not. He allows that external goods and plain luck matter, that a life can be damaged by misfortune, and that happiness needs a complete life to be judged. The four-word version quietly deletes all of that.
detailsBody: Greek (I.9, 1099b): ‘and these things would be in agreement with what was said at the beginning.’
Ross (public domain): ‘and this will be found to agree with what we said at the outset.’
Thomson (1955, in copyright): ‘The conclusion that happiness depends upon ourselves is in harmony with what I said in the first of these lectures.’
As quoted today: ‘Happiness depends upon ourselves. — Aristotle’ — the clause alone, with a citation it cannot support.
context.pull: The Greek contains no word for happiness, and none for ourselves.
